content: An abortifacient is a substance that induces abortion. History The ancient Greek colony of Cyrene once had an economy heavily reliant on the production and export of silphium, a potent abortifacient belonging to the parsley family. Silphium was so integral to Cyrene's wealth that its image was featured on both sides of the coins minted in the region. This plant, which was native only to a specific part of Libya, was overharvested by the Greeks, leading to its extinction. However, this standard theory of extinction has been challenged by alternative hypotheses, ranging from climate-related extinction to the possibility that silphium was not a single species but rather a composite of herbs, with its attribution to one species potentially being a deliberate misinformation effort. As the Catholic Church gained influence over European society, women who provided abortifacient herbs were often labeled as witches and subjected to persecution, as seen during the witch hunts. Present Time Herbal Abortifacients Many herbs and plants available over the counter today may act as abortifacients. These include wild carrot, black cohosh, slippery elm, pennyroyal, nutmeg, mugwort, papaya, vervain, common rue, and tansy. Typically, the labeling on these products advises against use by pregnant women but does not explicitly explain the reason for this warning. There is no reliable data on the efficacy of these plants in humans, although some animal studies have shown them to be effective. The use of herbs to induce abortion is strongly discouraged due to the risk of severe side effects. The 1898 edition of King’s American Dispensatory recommended a mixture of brewer’s yeast and pennyroyal tea as a safe and certain abortive. In the 1970s, prior to the Roe v. Wade decision, an older remedy for unwanted pregnancy involved the use of Vitamin C. A book titled A Woman’s Book of Choices: Abortion, Menstrual Extraction, RU-486 by Rebecca Chalker and Carol Downer suggested taking 6–10 grams of ascorbic acid (pure Vitamin C) daily for 5–10 days. Pharmaceutical Abortifacients Mifepristone, a competitive antagonist of the progesterone receptor, was first approved in 1988 under the trade name Mifegyne for the medical termination of early pregnancy when used in conjunction with a prostaglandin analogue. Misoprostol, a synthetic prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) analogue, was also approved in 1988 under the trade name Cytotec for reducing the risk of NSAID-induced gastric ulcers. In France, misoprostol is approved under the trade name GyMiso for use with mifepristone in medical abortion. Misoprostol alone is sometimes used for self-induced abortion in Latin American countries where legal abortion is unavailable, as well as by some immigrants from these countries in the United States who cannot afford a legal abortion. Pre-implantation Labeling Controversy Certain substances may prevent the implantation of a blastocyst, thereby terminating a pregnancy, even though their primary known effect is to prevent fertilization. The existence of these post-fertilization mechanisms is debated. There is ongoing controversy regarding whether pregnancy begins at the moment of fertilization or at the moment the blastocyst implants in the uterine lining. American federal law and British law define the beginning of pregnancy at implantation. Consequently, even if post-fertilization mechanisms were proven, these substances would still be classified as contraceptives rather than abortifacients. The following birth control methods have been proposed to sometimes prevent the implantation of a blastocyst, although they primarily work by preventing fertilization: Hormonal contraceptives Intrauterine devices (IUDs) The lactational amenorrhea method, which may cause a luteal phase defect (LPD). LPD can interfere with the implantation of embryos. Fertility awareness methods: A philosophy professor has speculated that intercourse during the less-fertile times of the cycle might result in embryos incapable of implanting due to aged gametes at the time of fertilization. Some herbal contraceptives may primarily work by preventing implantation.
